titulo.texto: Monument 21: The Woman of the Stela

frase_gancho.texto: A woman standing before a tall pillar: one of the few female images in this art.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow your route: the tour moves on toward other stones of the settlement and the hill.

guion_corto.texto: A standing woman stretches out both arms to touch a tall pillar. This is Monument Twenty-one, a stela. On her head she wears a headdress like a kerchief that falls down her back almost to the ground. She stands on the face of a supernatural earth being. Images of women are uncommon in the art of this period. Here she is not the only one: at least two other stelae with women in the same posture and the same attire have been excavated. David Grove wonders, without asserting it, whether this figure is related to the tomb of an elite woman, found with a stone head, Monument Seventeen.

guion_largo.texto:
Images of women are uncommon in this art. That is why this monument draws attention. Monument Twenty-one is a stela that shows a standing woman. Grove cites it as a good example of a feature of the set: it includes images of women, something uncommon.

The scene is simple to describe. The woman stretches both arms to touch a tall pillar. Her head is covered by a headdress like a kerchief that extends down her back almost to the ground. And she stands on the face of a supernatural earth being.

What exactly the pillar represents is something the sources consulted do not specify. Nor do they explain what she is doing. What we do know is that it is not an isolated case. Córdova Tello and Meza Rodríguez reported, in two thousand seven, that in this part of the site at least two more stelae were excavated. They have female images, in the same posture and with the same attire.

For archaeologists, that repetition matters. A repeated image stops being one sculptor's whim and becomes a formula. Someone in this community wanted women to be seen with that posture and that headdress.

A stela is a tall, carved stone that is set upright. Those on the terraces, says Grove, deal above all with the political power of elite individuals. That there are women among them is part of what makes this site special.

Notice how the image is organized. Below, the face of an earth being. Above it, the standing woman. And in front of her, the tall pillar that she touches with both arms. They are three elements that read from the bottom up.

Like most of the sculptures on the terraces, this stela is from the Middle Preclassic. These sculptures appeared in the excavations of the Chalcatzingo Archaeological Project, in the area of the settlement and in the terraced fields.

There is another find that invites questions. When excavating an elite house of the period, Grove and his team found a stone-lined tomb beneath the floor. It contained vessels, a few badly eroded bones, and a stone head, Monument Seventeen. From the excavation data, it appears to be the tomb of an elite woman.

Grove raises a question with caution: is that head the portrait of the person buried? And he proposes that it could be the image of a dead woman, who apparently is represented in Monument Twenty-one. It is a possibility, not a proven fact.

One more detail to place this art. There was a decapitated statue of a seated figure, Monument Sixteen, which Eulalia Guzmán documented in nineteen thirty-four. Today it is displayed in the National Museum of Anthropology. The head of Monument Seventeen is not the one it is missing.

On the terraces there are other very particular stones, some pairs of altar and stela: [the round altars and the stelae](chz_10_altares_y_estelas).

texto.pregunta: Myth: In the art of that period only men appeared.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Chalcatzingo has images of women, such as Monument Twenty-one; Grove points out that this is uncommon.
